lesson.title: One Ancestor, Many Forms: Adaptive Radiation
lesson.summary: Adaptive radiation is the relatively rapid diversification of a single ancestral lineage into many descendant species, each adapted to a different ecological niche, often triggered by colonization of a new environment or the disappearance of competitors.
lesson.body:
Adaptive radiation describes a pattern rather than a single mechanism: a single ancestral species gives rise, over a relatively short span of evolutionary time, to many descendant species that differ from each other mainly in how they are adapted to different ecological niches, different food sources, different habitats, or different ways of making a living. It is best understood as the combined outcome of the speciation processes you have already studied, allopatric speciation, sympatric speciation, or often a mix of both occurring repeatedly, together with strong natural selection pushing each new lineage toward a different ecological specialty.

The conditions that tend to trigger adaptive radiation share a common theme: an unusual abundance of ecological opportunity combined with reduced competition. This happens classically when a species colonizes a new island or archipelago that has empty ecological niches and few or no competitors already using them. It can also happen after a mass extinction clears out previously dominant groups, opening up niches for survivors to diversify into, or after a lineage evolves a genuine biological innovation, such as a new way of feeding or moving, that lets it exploit resources no competitor can reach.

The single most famous example, and the one that helped inspire Darwin's thinking about evolution by natural selection, is the group of finches now known as Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands. You met the geographic side of this story in the allopatric speciation chapter: a single ancestral finch population from the South American mainland colonized the islands and became fragmented by the ocean separating them. What makes this a textbook case of adaptive radiation specifically is what happened ecologically once those island populations were established. Arriving on islands with few competing bird species and a wide variety of unexploited food sources, from hard seeds to insects to cactus flowers, descendants of that single ancestral finch diversified into more than a dozen recognized species, distinguished most strikingly by the shape and size of their beaks. Species with large, deep beaks specialize on cracking tough seeds, species with thin, pointed beaks specialize on insects, and one species even uses cactus spines as tools to pry insects out of crevices. Each beak shape is a direct adaptation to a particular food source, and researchers, notably Peter and Rosemary Grant in decades of fieldwork on the islands, have directly measured natural selection acting on beak size and shape from one generation to the next as food availability shifted with changing weather conditions.

A second well documented case involves the Hawaiian honeycreepers, a group of birds descended from a single ancestral finch-like colonist that reached the Hawaiian Islands. Over time this lineage diversified into a striking range of species with bill shapes adapted for very different feeding strategies, some curved for probing tubular flowers for nectar, some thick and finch-like for crushing seeds, and some suited for gleaning insects from bark, occupying ecological roles filled by entirely different, unrelated bird families elsewhere in the world. Unfortunately many honeycreeper species have gone extinct or become endangered in recent history, largely because of introduced predators, habitat loss, and introduced diseases like avian malaria, but the surviving diversity still illustrates the same underlying pattern of one ancestor diversifying to fill many available niches.

It is worth being clear about how adaptive radiation relates to the concepts building up to it. Adaptive radiation is not a distinct type of speciation alongside allopatric and sympatric speciation, it describes many rounds of speciation, by whichever mechanism, happening in a burst and being channeled by natural selection into a diversity of ecological specialties rather than producing species that merely differ incidentally. This ecological angle, the idea that diversification is driven by fitting different lineages into different niches, is also the concept that connects most directly to the next chapter, convergent evolution, where you will see that unrelated lineages placed under similar ecological pressures can independently evolve strikingly similar solutions, essentially the mirror image of what happens when one lineage radiates into many different niches.
